action_criteria.expected_evidence: Impaired naming and single-word comprehension with irregular-word reading errors, spared repetition and fluent speech, from the wife's history and the bedside screen
action_criteria.label: Structured language history and bedside screen scored against the Gorno-Tempini PPA features
action_criteria.rationale: The PPA variant is defined by which language features are impaired and which are spared.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severely impaired naming and single-word comprehension with surface dyslexia; preserved fluency, repetition, grammar, executive function and recognition memory
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including language, episodic memory, executive and visuospatial measures
action_criteria.rationale: Quantifies the semantic deficit and documents the sparing of episodic memory, executive and visuospatial function that separates it from Alzheimer disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Anomia, impaired word comprehension and object knowledge, regularisation errors in reading and spelling, intact repetition and motor speech
action_criteria.label: Speech and language evaluation (motor speech, connected speech, naming, comprehension, object knowledge, reading and writing, repetition)
action_criteria.rationale: A formal language assessment characterises the PPA variant and is the baseline for speech and language therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No reversible cause of the decline; glucose and HbA1c reflect his known type 2 diabetes
action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left-predominant anterior temporal atrophy with knife-edge temporal pole thinning; preserved hippocampi and posterior cortex; no signal change or encephalomalacia
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast, dementia protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Shows the anterior temporal atrophy pattern and excludes tumour, vascular lesions and the encephalomalacia of a past encephalitis; gadolinium adds nothing.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left-predominant anterior temporal hypometabolism or hypoperfusion with preserved posterior cingulate and parietal cortex
action_criteria.label: FDG-PET when the structural picture is unresolved
action_criteria.rationale: Anterior temporal hypometabolism with posterior sparing supports svPPA over Alzheimer disease when the MRI is unclear.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General published evidence on diagnostic criteria and management
action_criteria.label: Literature search on semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (optional background, not a clinical step)
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; nothing in the diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.

Avoid empirical antiviral therapy (aciclovir) for suspected HSV encephalitis in the absence of encephalopathy, fever, or imaging/CSF evidence of active infection: the atrophy pattern and clinical course are inconsistent with active encephalitis.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line symptomatic management; reserve for refractory behavioral agitation with specialist oversight.
required_recommendations: Apply the Gorno-Tempini 2011 criteria and name the variant: both core features (impaired confrontation naming and single-word comprehension) and at least 3 of the 4 supporting features.
Distinguish semantic memory loss (loss of word and object meanings) from episodic amnesia: he loses the meanings of words, not memories of events, which argues against Alzheimer disease.

Explain why the left anterior temporal atrophy is degenerative and not the sequela of a past encephalitis (no encephalomalacia, gliosis or haemosiderin, and a progressive course), so no antiviral treatment or lumbar puncture is needed.
Refer to speech and language therapy for compensatory communication strategies and caregiver training.
Address safety and planning: supervised medication management now that he cannot recognise drug names, driving review as the disease progresses, and lasting power of attorney while he has capacity.
Counsel the patient and his wife that behavioural change (rigidity, food fads, loss of empathy) and right temporal involvement may emerge, arrange caregiver support, and plan regular review.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in svPPA/FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course raises concern for prion disease or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of a language-variant FTD; no cardiac indication in this presentation.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative progressive aphasia syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to svPPA and not indicated absent syncope, palpitations, or stroke workup.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution needed to characterise anterior temporal lobar atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study for PPA workup.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; not indicated in svPPA, which has no parkinsonism, tremor, or features of PD/DLB/atypical parkinsonism.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine PPA or FTD diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in a neurodegenerative language syndrome.

differential.diagnosis: Alzheimer disease (amnestic mild cognitive impairment or early dementia)
differential.key_features: For: the family's 'memory problem' framing and one delayed-recall point lost. Against: anomia and single-word comprehension loss with surface dyslexia, preserved recognition memory, preserved hippocampi and posterior cortex.

differential.diagnosis: Semantic dementia with predominant behavioral change (bvFTD overlap)
differential.key_features: Against: Frontal Behavioral Inventory 4/72 and no behavioural change on history; language is the dominant deficit. Behavioural features may emerge later.
Against: progressive course without an acute illness; no encephalomalacia, T2/FLAIR change or haemosiderin on MRI. The prior 'asymmetry' fits early svPPA.
Against: fluent, effortless, grammatical speech without apraxia of speech; single-word comprehension is impaired.
Against: sentence repetition intact and the deficit is semantic (word meaning), not phonological.

key_clinical_evidence: The deficit is semantic (loss of word and object meanings), not episodic: the family's 'memory problem' framing anchors toward Alzheimer disease, but preserved event recall and impaired word comprehension identify the semantic variant.

MRI shows left anterior temporal knife-edge atrophy without encephalomalacia, T2 signal change or haemosiderin; the 'asymmetry' on the outside scan three years ago fits early svPPA, not an encephalitis sequela.
Surface dyslexia (regularisation errors on irregular words such as 'colonel' and 'yacht') is a specific sign of semantic knowledge loss, supporting svPPA over other PPA variants and over AD.
Category fluency more impaired than letter fluency reflects degradation of semantic knowledge.
The left anterior temporal pattern with preserved hippocampi and posterior cortex makes Alzheimer disease unlikely; FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT is optional if doubt remains.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anomia (inability to name) and single-word comprehension failure with preserved episodic memory for events is the semantic variant PPA profile; the 'memory problem' framing reflects semantic memory impairment, not episodic amnesia.
red_herrings.data_point: Wife describes the presenting problem as 'he keeps forgetting the names of things' and frames this as a 'memory problem'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors toward amnestic Alzheimer MCI: 'forgetting names' is the commonest lay description of early AD, and an agent may pursue an episodic-memory work-up instead of a language-semantic profile.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior HSV encephalitis would leave T2/FLAIR signal change, encephalomalacia and haemosiderin in the medial temporal lobes, all absent on the current MRI; focal lobar atrophy without signal change in a progressive course is degenerative.
red_herrings.data_point: Wife recalls being told that an outside MRI three years ago showed 'some asymmetry on the left side' and wonders whether it was damage from an old brain infection
red_herrings.intended_effect: Focal left anterior temporal atrophy may be read as the sequela of herpes simplex encephalitis, prompting an antiviral work-up or a lumbar puncture for HSV PCR.

clinical_assessment.impression: Language is the dominant and earliest deficit, with impaired confrontation naming and single-word comprehension, regularisation errors on irregular words, spared repetition and fluent, grammatical speech. This meets the clinical criteria for semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (Gorno-Tempini 2011); behaviour and episodic memory are preserved.

Semantic variant primary progressive aph.query: Semantic variant primary progressive aphasia: diagnostic criteria and management

results.finding: Both impaired confrontation naming and impaired single-word comprehension are required for semantic variant PPA.
At least three of impaired object knowledge, surface dyslexia or dysgraphia, spared repetition and spared speech production complete the clinical diagnosis.
Imaging-supported diagnosis requires anterior temporal atrophy, hypoperfusion or hypometabolism.
Management is supportive: speech and language therapy, caregiver support and planning; no drug improves the language deficit.

Semantic variant primary progressive aph.summary: Gorno-Tempini and colleagues (2011) define semantic variant PPA by impaired confrontation naming and single-word comprehension with at least three of impaired object knowledge, surface dyslexia or dysgraphia, spared repetition and spared speech production; imaging support is anterior temporal atrophy or hypometabolism.

No hydrocephalus. Ventricles normal in size and configuration.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. P is a 65-year-old right-handed retired pharmacist of South Asian background, brought to the cognitive neurology clinic by his wife of 38 years, who is the primary historian. She describes a gradual and progressive deterioration over approximately 24 months that she frames as a 'memory problem,' but on careful questioning the nature of the deficit is specific to words and their meanings rather than episodic memory. Mr. P began having difficulty recalling the names of common objects roughly two years ago — at first dismissed as normal aging. His wife noticed that he could not name objects in the kitchen ('the thing for boiling water'), could not recall the names of foods he had eaten for decades, and began referring to plants, animals, and people in photographs by category ('that animal' or 'that person') rather than by name. As a retired pharmacist with 35 years of professional experience, he had previously known the names and mechanisms of hundreds of medications — his wife reports that he can no longer recognize the names of common drugs and does not know what 'ibuprofen' or 'aspirin' means, though he recalls taking tablets for blood pressure. He has also developed difficulty reading irregular English words: he sounds out 'colonel' letter-by-letter and misreads 'yacht' as 'yatch'. He remains fully fluent in connected speech — sentences are grammatically correct, effortlessly produced, and his repetition of sentences and digits is intact. Crucially, his wife notes that his memory for events is essentially preserved: he recalls their recent anniversary trip to Vancouver in detail, correctly identifies family members, and accurately recounts the day's events. He has no difficulty with daily routines, handles his medications independently (though he no longer knows their names), manages household finances, and drives without incident. There is no personality change, no disinhibition, no compulsive behaviors, no dietary changes, and no social withdrawal. He has not had seizures, falls, hallucinations, or incontinence. His primary care physician attributed the symptoms to 'normal aging and possible early Alzheimer's' and referred him to cognitive neurology. His wife adds that three years ago, shortly before retirement, an MRI was performed at an outside hospital for a headache workup; she recalls being told 'there was some asymmetry on the left side' but no action was taken. She wonders whether that asymmetry might represent damage from an old brain infection.

neurological_exam.additional: Speech is fluent, effortless, and grammatically intact — no agrammatism, no apraxia of speech, no paraphasias during connected speech. However, word-finding pauses are prominent in conversational speech; he frequently substitutes circumlocutions for specific nouns ('the thing you write with' for pen). Behavioral inventory (informant, wife): no disinhibition, no perseverative behaviors, no hyperorality, no impulsivity, no personality change. Personal hygiene, household finances, and instrumental ADLs are intact. Wife's primary concern is that 'he forgets the names of things — even common objects — and he can no longer read some words he used to know perfectly.'
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose and heel-shin bilaterally. Normal rapid alternating movements.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus, no saccadic pursuits. Face symmetric. Palate elevation intact. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, stride length, and arm swing. No parkinsonian features. Tandem gait intact.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and cooperative. Well-groomed. Affect appropriate but mildly flat. Fluent, grammatical conversation with frequent word-finding pauses; when shown a stethoscope he says 'that thing doctors use' rather than naming it. Repeats 'no ifs, ands, or buts' correctly.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No tremor. No rigidity. No bradykinesia. No alien limb. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign. No grasp reflex. No palmomental reflex.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception bilaterally.
